analysis.one_liner: Requires dietary supplement makers to list products and ingredients with the FDA in a public database.
analysis.headline: Introduced with bipartisan sponsorship in April 2022, the bill never received a committee hearing or vote and died when the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require every company that sells a dietary supplement to register that product with the FDA, disclosing its ingredients, warnings, health claims, and where it is made. The FDA would assign each supplement a unique ID and post the information in a searchable public database so shoppers could see what is actually in the products they buy. Supplements sold without registration would be considered misbranded and illegal to sell.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers of dietary supplements, used by a large share of American adults, gain the ability to look up a product's actual ingredients, warnings, and manufacturing locations in a public FDA database. The FDA gains a basic roster of what is being sold, which makes it far easier to trace problem products during recalls or contamination outbreaks. Honest manufacturers also benefit, because competitors hiding ingredients would have to disclose them or leave the market.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers who take vitamins and supplements

how_it_helps.text: Requires the company responsible for each supplement to register it with the FDA, disclosing all label ingredients and amounts, conditions of use, warnings, allergen statements, health-related claims, and every facility where the product is made, packaged, or held.
Directs the FDA to create a publicly accessible, searchable electronic database so anyone can look up registered supplement information by product identifier or other fields.
Makes any supplement that was required to be listed but was not listed 'misbranded' under federal food law, giving the FDA a straightforward way to pull unregistered products off the market.

Requires manufacturers to keep records of where they get their ingredients and turn them over to the FDA within 72 hours of a request, which helps trace contaminated or adulterated products back to their source.

Makes it a prohibited act to sell a supplement prepared with the help of, or at the direction of, a person debarred from FDA proceedings, closing a loophole for products from companies with a history of violations.

analysis.who_pays: Dietary supplement manufacturers bear new compliance costs: registering every product and reformulation, reporting discontinuations, and maintaining supplier records, with civil and criminal exposure for selling unlisted products. Some of that cost would likely be passed to consumers in prices. The Treasury also funds FDA implementation, authorized at $4 million for fiscal 2022 and $1 million per year through 2026.

drawbacks.text: Listing is not safety review. The bill does not require the FDA to test supplements or approve them before sale, and it expressly states it should not be construed to expand the FDA's existing authorities beyond the listing requirement, so a listed product could still be ineffective or unsafe.

The compliance burden falls on every manufacturer, including small supplement companies, which must file detailed listings for each product and each reformulation within tight deadlines; some of that cost would likely reach consumers through higher prices.

A public database could give shoppers a false sense of security, since registration shows only what a company filed about its own product; the FDA is not verifying the claims when it assigns the listing.

Funding for the new system is modest — $4 million for fiscal 2022 and $1 million per year through 2026 — which raises a real question about whether the FDA could build and maintain the database on that budget.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but narrow: shoppers would finally be able to see what is in a supplement and where it was made, and the FDA would know what is being sold, which matters during recalls and contamination events. The costs are modest compliance paperwork for industry and a small appropriation for the FDA. The bill's honest weakness is that it stops at transparency — it does not require any testing or premarket approval, so the worst products on the market would simply become documented rather than prohibited. Still, disclosure is the foundation for every later enforcement step, and the costs are small relative to a supplement market measured in the tens of billions of dollars.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate health committee on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Dick Durbin introduced the bill on April 26, 2022, joined by Senator Mike Braun, a Republican, giving it bipartisan sponsorship from the start.
The same day, the bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
No further action of any kind appears in the record — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action — and the bill died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Dietary supplement manufacturers came out ahead: they continue selling products with no requirement to disclose ingredients, manufacturing locations, or claims to the FDA, and shoppers never got the public database. Consumers who take supplements are the losers, since a basic transparency tool never became available.

for.name: Dick Durbin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and sponsored it; has been the Senate's leading advocate for requiring supplement makers to list products with the FDA.

for.name: Mike Braun
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, making it a bipartisan introduction.

against.name: Patty Murray
against.role: Chair, Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a committee hearing or markup; it sat in committee from the day of introduction until the Congress ended.

against.name: Dietary supplement industry trade groups
against.what_they_did: Opposed mandatory FDA product listing, which Durbin had repeatedly proposed in prior Congresses; the industry has long lobbied against a listing mandate as a step toward treating supplements more like drugs.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's only two sponsors were one Democrat and one Republican, and no vote was ever taken, so no partisan split ever appeared on the record.

industries.note: Every seller would have to register each product with the FDA, disclose ingredients, warnings, claims, and facilities, and keep supplier records — and selling an unlisted product would become illegal. The industry profits today from a regime where no one outside the company needs to know exactly what is in a bottle, so its interest runs against the transparency shoppers would gain.

Brand owners would have to record the name and address of every supplier they buy ingredients from and hand that list to the FDA within 72 hours of a request, pulling a layer of the supply chain out of anonymity. The disclosure burden is modest but unwelcome for firms that currently operate behind their customers.
